summary: This standards-track document carries the image body parts originally defined in RFC 1495, for image formats first defined in MIME, through an X.400 system.

plainLanguage.summary: Making sure pictures stay pictures when mail passes through an older mail system.

questions: how is jpeg carried in x.400
subtitle: Defines how JPEG and GIF images are carried through X.400 mail and mapped to their MIME types.

tldr.problem: JPEG and GIF image formats were defined in MIME, but X.400 mail systems needed matching body parts to carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a JPEG and a GIF Extended Body Part, each a plain octet string with an object identifier, and lists how they map to the MIME types image/jpeg and image/gif with no conversion.
tldr.outcome: Images can pass between MIME and X.400 unchanged. The RFC also records the FTAM object identifiers for the same formats, which it expects to be more useful.

today: RFC 2158 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content:
This document carries the body parts defined in RFC 1495 for image formats that were originally defined in MIME through an X.400 system.

It also documents the object identifiers (OIDs) assigned to these formats as FTAM body parts, so the MIME types can be converted to FTAM body parts. The RFC says this will probably be more useful than the new body parts it defines.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mail systems speak different languages. This note gives picture files a name tag in the older one.

sections.title: The JPEG and GIF Body Parts
sections.content:
Two new Extended Body Parts are defined, jpeg-body-part and gif-body-part. Both have no parameters, and their data is an OCTET STRING whose content is as defined in MIME.

Each is identified by an object identifier under mixer-bp-data: JPEG is { mixer-bp-data 3 } and GIF is { mixer-bp-data 4 }.
sections.plainLanguage: Each picture type gets its own numbered label, and the picture bytes go inside untouched.

sections.title: Equivalences with MIME Types
sections.content:
Four equivalences are listed, all with conversion type "None". The image/jpeg type maps to the JPEG Extended Body Part and to the FTAM EMA JPEG body part. The image/gif type maps to the GIF Extended Body Part and to the FTAM EMA GIF body part.

The EMA JPEG OID is built from the EMA organization identifier and works out to the numeric form { 2 16 840 1 113694 2 2 1 6 }. The EMA GIF OID ends in gif-image(4) under the same EMA prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: A table says which old-system label matches which new-system label. Because the picture bytes are the same, nothing has to be changed on the way across.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC says only that security issues are not considered in this memo. It adds no security mechanism of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The note does not say anything about keeping pictures secret or safe.
